title: Optimal scaling laws in learning hierarchical multi-index models
claim: Learning error follows power-law decay in sample ratio, with rates set by target feature structure, and theory matches finite-size experiments.
layout: 1 panel, log-log plot, three colored curves, dashed slope guides annotated with exponents
description: A single log-log plot. The x-axis is the sample ratio alpha = n/d, running from 10^0 to about 3000. The y-axis is a weighted mean squared error, MSE_gamma, falling from 1 to roughly 0.004. Three curves are drawn with solid lines and overlaid markers: blue circles, green squares and orange diamonds. The legend at lower left gives a different link function g(z) for each curve: tanh(z^2) centered, |z| centered, and a combination of Hermite polynomials He2 and He4. Every curve starts on a plateau at 1 and then bends into a power-law decay. The blue curve plateaus longest and decays slowest, and the orange curve decays fastest. Two gray dashed reference lines carry slope labels, alpha^{-1+1/(2 gamma)} near the top and alpha^{-1} near the bottom right. Markers lie on the solid lines, so theory and simulation agree. The eye goes first to the curves and the slope annotations.
caption: Weighted mean square error ${\rm MSE}_\gamma$ -- see Def. [ref] -- of the spectral estimator of Def. [ref] with preprocessing function $\cT(y)=y/(1+|y|)$. The target is given by the hierarchical multi-index model [ref], with $g_k(z)=g(z)\; \forall k$, stated in the legend, and $a_k^\star \propto k^{-\gamma}$, $\gamma = 1$. Solid lines: asymptotic prediction for $d\to\infty$, from Theorem [ref] and the overlaps derived in App. [ref]. Dots represent averages over $30$ instances, for covariates with dimension $d = 2000$, feature space dimension $m_\star = 10$ and label noise variance $\Delta = 0.5$.
abstract: In this work, we provide a sharp theory of scaling laws for two-layer neural networks trained on a class of hierarchical multi-index targets, in a genuinely representation-limited regime. We derive exact information-theoretic scaling laws for subspace recovery and prediction error, revealing how the hierarchical features of the target are sequentially learned through a cascade of phase transitions. We further show that these optimal rates are achieved by a simple, target-agnostic spectral estimator, which can be interpreted as the small learning-rate limit of gradient descent on the first-layer weights. Once an adapted representation is identified, the readout can be learned statistically optimally, using an efficient procedure. As a consequence, we provide a unified and rigorous explanation of scaling laws, plateau phenomena, and spectral structure in shallow neural networks trained on such hierarchical targets.
